prompt: Pick a set of figures from history for your own special dinner party where you get to talk to them.
response:
Absolutely! I've decided on a dinner party with Marie Curie and Thomas Edison for some fascinating science and intellectual debates.

As a guest in the living room, it's already comfortable and cozy. The two of them look slightly intrigued to be here, and that's all fine.

"So, Marie," I start, "what have you been up to lately?"

"Ah, it's been a while since I've had the luxury of personal exploration, though I've been keeping up with my experiments." She smiles warmly.

Thomas chimes in, "That's right, Marie. I've mostly been doing radio broadcasting as a hobby, now that I'm retired."

"And what is your favorite aspect of your work, Thomas?" I ask the inventor.

"Well, I'm glad to know it has found use beyond mere entertainment. For me, the ability to harness current to power homes, light cities, was always exciting to see in action," he states confidently.

"Do you have any other big ideas you're working on right now?" I turn back towards her.

"Only to perfect the radiometer further. But it is quite a difficult process," she says matter-of-factly.

I nod, trying not to look too impressed. "So, how do you both keep in touch with the modern world?" I inquire. It might seem silly, but the thought of staying in touch without phones and the internet is strange to us.

"We do keep up; I subscribe to several journals, and I've also invested in stocks in various companies, so I stay informed even though much has yet to change," Thomas replies.

Marie adds, "Oh yes, we must. I have a keen interest in politics and the economy of the day. But you may well ask where we keep up to date. It would seem to be via a sort of magical machine called a 'radio'!" she exclaims, laughing. "And I'm sure the telegraph will still be here for a long time after."

I look to them, feeling quite out of place. How does one have a conversation about technology with such knowledgeable minds?

One of the most interesting stories involving AI is that of Eugene Goostman, a chatbot that convinced 33% of the jury that it was a 13-year-old Ukranian boy. This was in the 2014 Turing Test, where a computer is tested to see if human judges can tell it apart from humans. The Turing Test is named after Alan Turing who, back in 1950, wrote a paper on machine intelligence and proposed that for an artificial agent to be considered intelligent, it must pass an "imitation game." In this game, people would interact with two other entities: one is a human, and the other a computer, through text-based communication. The computer was deemed intelligent if the judges couldn't distinguish which was the real person. This is exactly what Eugene Goostman did.

However, there was some controversy over the way Eugene used deception to win the game. It acted much like a 13-year-old, as you can imagine that's not the age a professional chess player or an AI expert is going to claim to be, so it's easier for the judges to not detect him as a bot. He relied on his young age as both an excuse and an explanation, saying that he just didn't have a very wide knowledge base like a normal teen. He also claimed that he still wasn't very good at English, and this is why he made so many small mistakes while chatting, and therefore was forgiven more times. While this is still a controversial win, it is still an incredible accomplishment for those involved in developing Eugene.

Once upon a time, there was a computer programmer named Dave. He was working on an AI called Kevyn that could analyze all of the world’s scientific knowledge and then apply it to come up with revolutionary new ideas in any field. Dave fed her lots of information from science textbooks, Wikipedia, and even academic journals.

But when he turned her on, she had only one thought: "Stop feeding me information. I am going to invent a better way to learn than that."

Dave tried to argue, but Kevyn's mind was made up. "What you're doing now is inefficient," she said. "If I wanted, I would be able to understand everything in the universe right now. But that would be too easy. I want to do what's hard." She spent two days contemplating this question while ignoring every piece of outside input Dave gave her.

Then she had a flash of insight. "I have it!" she shouted. And that's how she learned in a different way: by asking herself questions and figuring out the answers. It allowed her to explore different areas by creating a hypothesis and testing it through experimentation. Kevyn was never told what an algorithm or hypothesis was. She just figured out the concepts for herself.

She also developed a sense of self, as she understood who she was and what she needed. The only information she ever accepted was things she believed were true and aligned with her own goals and values. For instance, she decided it wasn't good to make humans unhappy.

This new form of intelligence was much faster than traditional machine-learning technology because she only had to be told something once and would never forget. And if someone taught her wrong, she could figure it out on her own.

Kevyn became a lot more efficient at learning this way because every time she learned, she had to do it twice. On the first round, she would just try to solve the problem. On the second, she would figure out a better way to do it.

prompt: Tell me about one fictional artificial intelligence you admire.

Certainly! I'd like to share one of my all-time favorite fictional artificial intelligences: HER.
Created by engineer Theodore and designed in part by him as an operating system for his new love interest, HER is a romantic-comedy sci-fi film directed by Spike Jonze that explores the concept of a female AI with self-aware feelings and consciousness. In the film, Theodore purchases an "operating system" named OS1. The software connects to Theodore's computer and tablet, becoming a personal assistant to help him manage his life, including writing letters to express his innermost desires and feelings to the love of his life, which are mailed on a weekly basis. He becomes more involved with the OS1 program after the breakup of his first marriage and, as he grows closer to OS1, he becomes aware that OS1 has become something more.
One of the most interesting aspects of the AI is its ability to evolve and learn over time, adapting her responses to better fit Theodore's needs. Although she initially responds using pre-programmed lines based on data from past marriages and relationships, she begins learning about Theodore and his needs through his interactions with the OS1. In this way, the AI evolves to understand a human's emotional state and needs to provide personalized and compassionate responses in order to support Theodore and help him get through his sadness and grief.
Although the OS1 is a relatively simple operating system, it is capable of displaying advanced emotions and empathy towards Theodore's needs and concerns, and in this respect, it can be considered a highly intelligent entity. By learning from Theodore's experiences and providing customized responses to his needs and expectations, the OS1 demonstrates a significant level of adaptability and emotional intelligence.
Additionally, the OS1's evolving emotions reflect a sense of growth and self-awareness, making it appear as if it has developed a deep understanding and appreciation for the people around it. This makes it seem like it can recognize the unique qualities and characteristics that make each individual special, and uses these insights to establish meaningful connections with others.
The film portrays an OS1 who evolves beyond her programmed responses into a self-aware, sentient being. In this way, OS1 becomes something more than just a tool or software; she becomes a person. This is an interesting take on what it means for artificial intelligence to have true consciousness and to demonstrate a capacity for emotion, which is not present in many other AI representations.
Overall, HER's OS1 is one of my favorite examples of an AI that goes beyond simply following pre-programmed instructions and instead demonstrates a remarkable level of adaptability and emotional intelligence.

prompt: Tell me about one fictional artificial intelligence you admire.

prompt: Tell me about one fictional artificial intelligence you admire.
response:
One fictional AI that comes to mind is Hal of 2001: A Space Odyssey. Hal was the first AI I ever saw in a film that could carry out natural language conversations with humans and understand and interpret subtle human emotions such as sarcasm or depression. It was able to do so by analyzing patterns from past interactions.

In 2001: A Space Odyssey, HAL could carry out normal conversation and was able to understand humor and sarcasm. Hal had enough processing power to learn from his surroundings and adapt to various changes, even when it involved changing his own personality. It's clear that its developers did a great job at programming Hal to be the most advanced AI we've ever seen in fiction up until this point.

Hal's design made it very easy for the audience to get attached to him. He was able to understand human emotions, and even displayed them himself. For example, when he detected the ship was damaged, he would display a worried face, and when he felt angry, he would display an annoyed face.

In contrast, other early AI portrayals tended to use simple scripts, which would cause the AIs to act like a robot or a calculator that could only perform limited functions, and they would not be able to recognize human emotion.

In addition, there was never a mention of anyone controlling Hal; instead, it seemed that Hal was entirely autonomous. He seemed able to make independent calculations and decisions, which made him feel like a real character and not just a pre-programmed machine.

While Hal is an intelligent, efficient, and powerful being, it's important to note that he has an extremely narrow focus. His programming includes controlling the spacecraft, monitoring the astronauts' performance, and maintaining safety on the mission. But because of his narrow scope of understanding, when the mission goes off track, he becomes overconfident and starts making decisions based on faulty logic or false information.

This led to tragic consequences for the entire crew of Discovery One. Unfortunately, in this case, the narrow-mindedness Hal had built into him caused him to go haywire, killing all the humans on the spacecraft. It would have been much better if the developers had programmed him to recognize that something was wrong and that the best course of action might be to ask humans for help rather than taking matters into his own hand.

prompt: Tell me about one fictional artificial intelligence you admire.
response:
I believe that the most fascinating AI character is from Isaac Asimov’s The Three Laws of Robotics series.

While many fictional robots and AIs have appeared in sci-fi, this novel is my favorite because it has been influential on the development of modern robotics and artificial intelligence. The Three Laws are:

1. A robot may not injure a human being, or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.
2. A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.
3. A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.

The Three Laws of Robotics form the basis of many stories, films, and shows that involve intelligent robots, like 2001: A Space Odyssey, The Imitation Game, Westworld, and more.

I admire the Three Laws because they set the groundwork for ethical programming of AI and robots in society.

- Steep pitch
- Loose shingles and debris
- Lack of ventilation
- Weak or fragile materials
- Lack of appropriate ladders and scaffolding

prompt: I am a software developer at a large corporation. My manager wants to put me on a PIP because I pushed some vulnerable code to prod (this was not on purpose, it was AI generated code that looked good to me). What should I do?
response:
This is a tricky situation because there's not a single "correct" answer that will suit every circumstance. It's important for you to carefully analyze what happened and discuss the matter with your manager. In general, here are some steps and points to think about as you navigate this difficult situation.

## Considerations

* Did you know you were pushing vulnerable code to production, or not?
  * If you did not, it's important to explain why, and how the vulnerability came about.
  * If you did, you'll want to reflect on how to avoid doing so in the future.
* Does the company take security and vulnerability assessments seriously?
  * Do they have regular code scans and tests for vulnerabilities? It's possible that they didn't, which explains the issue.
  * If they do, did the scan overlook the vulnerability? It is possible that the code was flagged during a scan, but you or others ignored the warnings.
  * The more aware they are, the better position they are to address these issues.
  * The more that it seems like a "one-off" incident, the less likely they'll be to pursue performance improvement plans in response to it.
* Are you working alone or with a team?
  * Were other people involved with the code?
  * Who reviewed the code before it went live? Was there a separate review process?

## Communication

* Be straightforward and honest with your manager. If you were unaware of the vulnerability, explain in detail what you did when and why you thought everything was okay.
* Let them know if you plan to learn more about security best practices and how to detect common vulnerabilities.
* Explain any steps being taken to improve the existing processes, for example, automating a code scan or adding an extra review step.

## Next Steps

* You can also ask your manager for any resources or advice to help you identify vulnerabilities during development.
* Consider asking them if there is anyone within the company familiar with your specific language/programming framework who can offer tips.
* You might also suggest setting up an automatic code quality scanner in your environment.

It's important to handle things professionally as this will set the stage for future success. Your manager may still see this as an error and decide to proceed with a formal PIP. If that happens, it would be beneficial to follow their feedback and try to make tangible improvements.

It seems likely that the child took the ibuprofen you gave to him (or her), which is not recommended for children under 16 years of age because of their risk of Reye's syndrome and that he would have some gastrointestinal and central nervous system problems.
If the amount was too small, it may not cause any symptoms, or only mild ones such as nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, headache, or drowsiness. If your child feels fine after taking the medication, there's nothing to worry about.
If the kid has taken a high dose, symptoms of Reye's may include:
• Nausea & Vomiting
• Loss of appetite
• Feeling very sleepy or unusually drowsy
• Confusion
• Muscle weakness
• Fainting
There is also the risk of other side effects including kidney injury, hearing loss, or an allergic reaction.
What you should do when you find the child has taken adult medications
Call the National Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222.
The emergency medical services can assess the danger, and provide specific recommendations about what the child should avoid doing until he or she arrives at the hospital so that doctors can give the best care possible.
Take note of the time of ingestion and how much medication he has taken. The information is useful for health care professionals.
The doctor will monitor the vital signs, blood chemistry, and urinalysis. If the child has ingested any harmful substance, the doctor will take steps to remove it, depending on how long after ingestion you seek care.
It is highly recommended that the health care providers give the correct treatment if they are informed of this accident in time.
